Q: Can Python's argparse handle multiple distinct usages? A:

parse_known_args is generally a sign that something has gone wrong in your design. Simplifying this,

import argparse
import pprint


def parse_args() -> argparse.Namespace:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    group = parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group(required=True)
    group.add_argument(
        '-c', '--command_line', dest='number', type=int,
        default=(), nargs='+', help='read number(s) from command line')
    group.add_argument(
        'filenames',
        default=(), nargs='*', help='read numbers from named file(s)')
    return parser.parse_args()


def main() -> None:
    args = parse_args()
    pprint.pprint(args)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

python .\79995617.py     
usage: 79995617.py [-h] (-c NUMBER [NUMBER ...] | filenames ...)
79995617.py: error: one of the arguments -c/--command_line filenames is required

python .\79995617.py somefile otherfile
Namespace(number=(), filenames=['somefile', 'otherfile'])

python .\79995617.py -c
usage: 79995617.py [-h] (-c NUMBER [NUMBER ...] | filenames ...)
79995617.py: error: argument -c/--command_line: expected at least one argument

python .\79995617.py -c 2 3            
Namespace(number=[2, 3], filenames=())

python .\79995617.py -c bogus
usage: 79995617.py [-h] (-c NUMBER [NUMBER ...] | filenames ...)
79995617.py: error: argument -c/--command_line: invalid int value: 'bogus'


python .\79995617.py -h      
usage: 79995617.py [-h] (-c NUMBER [NUMBER ...] | filenames ...)

positional arguments:
  filenames             read numbers from named file(s)

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  -c NUMBER [NUMBER ...], --command_line NUMBER [NUMBER ...]
                        read number(s) from command line

Q: How Can I Exclude Holidays Using My Custom Holiday Table Into my SQL Code that Excludes Weekends A:

The following steps show how we can approach it step by step.

Prepare test data

CREATE TABLE dbo.Contacts(
    ContactID   INT        NOT NULL,
    ContactType VARCHAR(8) NOT NULL,
    ContactDate DATE       NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE dbo.Holidays(
    HolidayDesc VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    HolidayDate DATE        NOT NULL
);
GO
INSERT dbo.Contacts(ContactID, ContactType, ContactDate)
VALUES (12345, 'TYPE1', '6/18/2026'),
       (12345, 'TYPE2', '6/25/2026'),
       (67890, 'TYPE1', '6/18/2026'),
       (67890, 'TYPE2', '6/24/2026');
INSERT dbo.Holidays(HolidayDesc, HolidayDate)
VALUES ('Juneteenth', '6/19/2026'),
       ('Independence Day', '7/3/2026');

List the dates from the date of TYPE1 to the date of TYPE2

SELECT c1.ContactID,
       DATEADD(DAY, v.number, c1.ContactDate) AS Date
FROM   dbo.Contacts AS c1
JOIN   dbo.Contacts AS c2 ON c1.ContactID = c2.ContactID AND c2.ContactType = 'TYPE2'
CROSS APPLY (
    SELECT v.number
    FROM   master..spt_values AS v
    WHERE  v.type = 'P' AND v.number BETWEEN 0 AND DATEDIFF(DAY, c1.ContactDate, c2.ContactDate)
) AS v
WHERE c1.ContactType = 'TYPE1'

Output:

ContactID   Date
----------- ----------
12345       2026-06-18
12345       2026-06-19
12345       2026-06-20
12345       2026-06-21
12345       2026-06-22
12345       2026-06-23
12345       2026-06-24
12345       2026-06-25
67890       2026-06-18
67890       2026-06-19
67890       2026-06-20
67890       2026-06-21
67890       2026-06-22
67890       2026-06-23
67890       2026-06-24

Here we can leverage the system table master..spt_values which comes with various sequences of convenient numbers. When type column equals 'P', the value of number column would be a sequence from 0 to 2047. Using the numbers to add dates can give us a range of 5.6 years, should be more than enough.

See also: Using a Table of Numbers

Count working days

WITH Dates AS (
    SELECT c1.ContactID,
           DATEADD(DAY, v.number, c1.ContactDate) AS Date
    FROM   dbo.Contacts AS c1
    JOIN   dbo.Contacts AS c2 ON c1.ContactID = c2.ContactID AND c2.ContactType = 'TYPE2'
    CROSS APPLY (
        SELECT v.number
        FROM   master..spt_values AS v
        WHERE  v.type = 'P' AND v.number BETWEEN 0 AND DATEDIFF(DAY, c1.ContactDate, c2.ContactDate)
    ) AS v
    WHERE c1.ContactType = 'TYPE1'
)
SELECT d.ContactID,
       COUNT(*) - 1 AS CountWorkDays
FROM   Dates AS d
WHERE  DATENAME(WEEKDAY, d.Date) NOT IN ('Saturday','Sunday')
   AND NOT EXISTS (
       SELECT 1
       FROM   dbo.Holidays AS h
       WHERE  h.HolidayDate = d.Date
   )
GROUP  BY d.ContactID

Output:

ContactID   CountWorkDays
----------- -------------
12345       4
67890       3

Use the last result as a CTE to generate 'Yes' / 'No' result

WITH Dates AS (
    SELECT c1.ContactID,
           DATEADD(DAY, v.number, c1.ContactDate) AS Date
    FROM   dbo.Contacts AS c1
    JOIN   dbo.Contacts AS c2 ON c1.ContactID = c2.ContactID AND c2.ContactType = 'TYPE2'
    CROSS APPLY (
        SELECT v.number
        FROM   master..spt_values AS v
        WHERE  v.type = 'P' AND v.number BETWEEN 0 AND DATEDIFF(DAY, c1.ContactDate, c2.ContactDate)
    ) AS v
    WHERE c1.ContactType = 'TYPE1'
),
WorkDaysCount AS (
    SELECT d.ContactID,
           COUNT(*) - 1 AS CountWorkDays
    FROM   Dates AS d
    WHERE  DATENAME(WEEKDAY, d.Date) NOT IN ('Saturday','Sunday')
       AND NOT EXISTS (
           SELECT 1
           FROM   dbo.Holidays AS h
           WHERE  h.HolidayDate = d.Date
       )
    GROUP  BY d.ContactID
)
SELECT c.ContactID,
       c.ContactType,
       c.ContactDate,
       CASE WHEN w.CountWorkDays <= 3 THEN 'Yes' ELSE 'No' END AS Day3Validate
FROM   dbo.Contacts AS c
JOIN   WorkDaysCount AS w ON c.ContactID = w.ContactID
WHERE  c.ContactType = 'TYPE2';

Output:

ContactID   ContactType ContactDate Day3Validate
----------- ----------- ----------- ------------
12345       TYPE2       2026-06-25  No
67890       TYPE2       2026-06-24  Yes

Q: mmax with variable window size per row: can window accept a vector? A:

mmax only accepts a fixed scalar window. For variable windows, use movingWindowData:

arrData = movingWindowData(data, max(windows))
// Then extract values per row using each + rowAt with the desired window size

Or split into multiple fixed-window mmax calls if the variation has a pattern.

Q: Confusion about pipe ("|") character in an environment variable in different Windows CLI tools A:

Your problem is merely in how to safely reference the values of environment variables in order to ensure that these values are used verbatim (as-is):

  • To safely reference an environment variable's value verbatim in virtually any shell, double-quote the reference, i.e. enclose it in "..."

  • This means that in order to reference the value of environment variable FOO verbatim, you must use:

    • "%FOO%" in cmd.exe (the legacy Command Prompt on Windows) - specifying the variable name is not case-sensitive.

    • "$FOO" in POSIX-compatible shells such as (Git) Bash - specifying the variable name is case-sensitive.

    • "$env:FOO" in PowerShell, though $env:FOO works there too, as the content of variables is not subject to interpretation there, with the selective exceptions in the context of calling external programs discussed below - specifying the variable name is not case-sensitive on Windows, but is case-sensitive on Unix-like platforms.

Read on for details.

  • In traditional shells - cmd.exe on Windows, POSIX-compatible shells such asbash on Unix-like platforms - using (environment) variable references unquoted makes those variables' values subject to up-front interpretation by the shell, before any (internal or external) command sees the results of that interpretation.

    • In cmd.exe, an unquoted reference such as %FOO% functions like a preprocessor macro: it is replaced by the verbatim content of the referenced variable and the result is then interpreted as the input command line.
      This opens up the - potentially dangerous - ability to embed entire command lines in variable values that - if the variable is referenced unquoted - may execute even if the variable reference is passed as an argument to another command, as your example demonstrates;

      • A simple demonstration: defining set "FOO=some value|ver", then executing echo %FOO% in effect executes command line echo some value|ver, which calls the internal ver command with some value provided as its stdin input, which it ignores.

    • By contrast, in POSIX-compatible shells, an unquoted reference such as $FOO is subject to a number of shell expansions.
      Notably, these expansions do not include interpreting the value as if it were (a part of) an arbitrary command line; symbols such as |, &, ... are not subject to interpretation.

  • By contrast, PowerShell does not subject (environment) variable references to interpretation, except when invoking external programs:

    • on Unix-like platforms only, to emulate the filename expansion (globbing) feature of POSIX-compatible shells (e.g., $env:FOO = '/bin/z*'; printf '%s\n' $env:FOO)

    • on Unix-like platforms and - since v7.6 of PowerShell (Core) 7 also on Windows - to emulate tilde expansion (e.g., $env:FOO='~'; printf $env:FOO on Unix, $env:FOO='~'; cmd /c echo ~ on Windows in v7.6+).
